title: Ability of detecting and willingness to share fake news
screen_reason: The paper's own aim (determinants of fake-news detection and willingness to share) is not prevalence, and the headline sharing measures are hypothetical intentions from a headline experiment, which are excluded. BUT Table 1 reports, as binary 0/1 proportions of the survey samples, two retrospective self-report items adapted from Barthel, Mitchell and Holcomb: 'Admits deliberate sharing' (ever shared a political news story online you thought at the time was made up) and 'Admits accidental sharing' (ever shared a political news story online you later found out was made up). These are shares of respondents who say they SHARED misinformation, i.e. RECALL (recall_subtype sharing), reported separately for Germany and the United Kingdom. Four such shares are extractable.

estimates.platform: Online survey (Qualtrics, administered by the panel company Respondi); the item asks about sharing a political news story 'online'
estimates.date: Second wave, 10 December 2021 to 14 December 2021 (first wave 3-30 March 2020; this paper uses wave 2)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report ever having shared a political news story online that they thought at the time was made up (deliberate sharing, self-reported)
estimates.denominator: 1,223 German respondents from the Respondi online panel, quota-sampled on gender, age, income and labour-market status
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'yes' to "Have you ever shared a political news story online that you thought at the time was made up?" (binary indicator, 1 = yes, 0 = no); lifetime window, asked before the headline task.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Fake news is pernicious as it spreads misleading and false information. Lazer et al. distinguish between misinformation (false or misleading information) and disinformation (false information that is purposely spread to deceive people)." The item itself operationalises fake news as a political news story that was 'made up'.
estimates.page_loc: Table 1, p. 3 (Descriptive statistics); item wording in Table 5 note, p. 7, and Methods 'Variables construction', p. 10
estimates.ground_truth_detail: No external verification: the respondent judges retrospectively whether a political news story they shared was 'made up'. The authors note the usual survey limitations (misunderstanding, dishonest answers) and elsewhere in the paper stress general overconfidence and social desirability in such reports.
estimates.moderator_quote: Finally, to elicit admitting of fake news sharing, we followed a public opinion poll previously conducted by Barthel, Mitchell, and Holcomb. In particular, participants were asked "Have you ever shared a political news story online that you thought at the time was made up?" to measure deliberate fake news sharing and "Have you ever shared a political news story online that you later found out was made up?" to measure accidental fake news sharing.
estimates.notes: Value read from Table 1's Mean/Prop. column for a 0/1 dummy, so the proportion is the share of respondents answering yes; expressed as a percentage (.035 = 3.5%). Deliberate and accidental admission are two different questions rather than stricter/broader versions of one another, so definition_variant is false for all four rows. Value read from Table 1 (Descriptive statistics, N = 2379); the quoted row gives Germany's Mean/Prop. (.035) then the United Kingdom's (.077).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The paper's headline sharing measures are HYPOTHETICAL: "Around 12 percent of respondents want to share at least one news item that they have correctly identified as fake news" and "More than 19 percent (17 percent in Germany, 21 percent in the UK) want to share accidentally", plus "In Germany, only 6 percent accidentally share three or more fake news headlines, whereas the percentage is 13 percent in the United Kingdom". These come from asking 'Would you consider sharing each of the following stories online...?' about five planted fake headlines — experimental sharing intentions, explicitly excluded by the protocol. Not extracted. (2) The detection outcome is a 0-40 scale reported only as a mean (Germany 23.662, UK 22.835) with no share of respondents above a threshold, so no row (scale means only). Likewise 'Sharing fake news' (0-10), 'Deliberate sharing' and 'Accidental sharing' (0-5) are scale means. (3) No estimate of exposure to or encountering of fake news is reported. (4) The France and Spain wave-1 samples are mentioned but not analysed here.

rob.design: Two national online surveys via Qualtrics, fielded by the panel provider Respondi to representative panels with quotas on gender, age, income and labour-market status; wave 2 fielded 10-14 December 2021 to wave-1 panel members, N = 2,379 (Germany 1,223; UK 1,156); no response rate reported; respondents dropped if they failed to complete the relevant part or finished in under 5 minutes or over two hours; mean completion 21 minutes; ethics approval from Zayed University Research Ethics Committee. Sample compared to Eurostat/national-statistics population values in Table 1 and noted to under-represent married/cohabiting people and 18-35s in both countries. The self-report sharing items are binary yes/no with no external validation; the authors acknowledge dishonest answering and misunderstanding as limitations.
